title: Is “generate → playtest → remix” actually a useful workflow for AI-assisted game dev?
author: Neon_Senpai
selftext:
I’m exploring an early concept around AI-assisted game creation, and I wanted to get feedback from people who actually build games with AI. The workflow I’m thinking about is not just “type a prompt and get a game,” because that feels too vague and usually not very useful.

A more practical loop might be:

idea → playable prototype → playtest → edit/remix → test again

For example, a user could start with something like “a cozy farming game with light puzzle mechanics,” then the system generates a small playable version. After trying it, they could change the rules, add a character, adjust the difficulty, remix the map, or turn it into a different genre.

So I’m curious how people here think about this from a real game dev perspective:

What part of this loop would actually be useful?

Would AI be more valuable for generating the first playable prototype, or for helping with iteration after playtesting?

What do you think is the hardest part to solve — gameplay logic, asset consistency, level design, balancing, or making the result actually fun?

Also, for solo devs or small teams, would a workflow like this help you prototype faster, or would it mostly create messy projects that still need too much manual cleanup?

No demo/link here, just trying to understand whether this direction makes sense before building too far in the wrong direction.

comments.author: TiToim
comments.body:
I would first work on a design prompt to get things right. It may even be an entire document. Then I would prompt it to build based on this document.


The big problem I found with Claude at least is that besides the first build and some major things it has diminishing returns and could have a largely bugged project.


So doing this first document is crucial for me.

replies.author: Neon_Senpai
replies.body:
That makes a lot of sense. I’m also leaning toward the idea that the “design document first” step is probably the part people underestimate the most.

The diminishing returns point is interesting too. A first AI-generated build can be useful as a rough prototype, but once the project gets bigger, bugs and messy structure become harder to fix through prompting alone. So maybe the better workflow is not “AI builds the whole game,” but “AI helps get a small playable version out quickly, then the human keeps the design/control tight.”

replies.author: Neon_Senpai
replies.body:
No, that’s a fair question — I probably should’ve explained it more clearly.

The “wrong direction” I had in mind is the common AI-tool trap where the product focuses too much on instant generation and not enough on whether the result is actually playable, testable, and worth improving. So instead of just “type prompt → get game,” I’m more interested in whether a platform could support the whole loop: create a quick prototype, get people to playtest it, collect useful feedback, then remix or iterate based on that.

And I totally agree that getting enough playtesters is one of the hardest parts. That might honestly be just as important as the generation part itself — a lot of solo devs don’t iterate enough because they don’t have people willing to test early versions.

comments.author: Aesthetic-Engine
comments.body:
It's more like:
1. Initial discussion with LLM to solidify:
-a north_star.md" file that describes what your final game looks like at a high level
- a AGENTS.md file that lists all the rules your agents must follow. This should be updated as you develop and find things the agents do that you don't like. It can be revised and carried over to every project you work on. Make sure you have language that says "build modularly, do not let the project assign all functions to a monolith/God object." Make sure you have agents commit all changes to git when they're done.

2. Deep research time. You need to ask your LLM what deep research prompts will produce information that will greatly help in developing your game. Run each of those prompts using Gemini (preferably) or ChatGPT deep research. Place the (exported as .md) papers in a folder called research. 

3. Synthesize research into .md files that define the different design aspects of the game. You and your LLM basically need to figure out what the files are that every agent needs to read before doing any work on the project. This keeps them from inventing game design/winging it.

4. Roadmap time. Have your LLM now built a roadmap for the project divided by "slices" that an agent can execute. That way you're building your game in pieces that can be cross-verified by another agent (instead of trying to magically build something cohesive in a handful of prompts.)

5. Now run each slice. Dont move onto the next slice till you play test and provide your agents with screenshots and bugs.

replies.author: Neon_Senpai
replies.body:
This is super helpful, thanks for laying it out so clearly.

The “north\_star.md” and “AGENTS.md” idea is especially interesting. It sounds like the real value is not just asking the AI to build, but giving it persistent project context, rules, and constraints so it doesn’t keep inventing or drifting away from the original design.

I also like the idea of building in slices and not moving forward until each slice has been playtested with screenshots/bugs. That feels much more realistic than expecting one big prompt to create something cohesive.

This makes me wonder if a platform like this should make the design brief / project rules / roadmap part of the creation flow, even for non-technical users, instead of hiding everything behind a single prompt box.

comments.author: SplinterOfChaos
comments.body:
>What do you think is the hardest part to solve — gameplay logic, asset consistency, level design, balancing, or making the result actually fun?

I feel that the actual hardest part that I don't hear often enough from the AI dev community is viability testing. Before AI, most games failed due to scope creep because game creators didn't know how to adapt their designs to the practical realities of development. AI isn't really helping there because as long as you have AI, everything seems equally viable. But at some point after a lot of work has gone into the project, that's when people realize that there was a limit to how far they could take it.

Again, this isn't really about AI, AI is just letting more people fail. And I don't mean that as a bad thing--you don't learn anything when you succeed because, clearly, you knew enough to succeed. Failure is what really makes you grow as a person. We need many people to try new things and fail so that we can also have people who try new things and succeed. Though I do worry that people who fail at something with AI are probably learning and improving a lot less than people who fail doing things by hand.

replies.author: Neon_Senpai
replies.body:
That’s a really good point. “Viability testing” is probably a better way to frame the hard part than just gameplay logic or asset consistency.

I agree that AI can make everything feel possible at the start, which might actually make scope creep worse. If a tool makes it easy to generate a bunch of ideas, but doesn’t help people figure out what is actually feasible, fun, and worth continuing, then it’s not solving the real problem.

Maybe the useful workflow needs to force smaller tests earlier: build a tiny playable slice, test whether the core idea works, get feedback, and only then expand. Otherwise people might spend a lot of time polishing something that was never viable as a game in the first place.

And yeah, I also think failing with AI can be less educational if people don’t understand why something failed. That’s something I’m thinking about too — the tool would need to help people learn from the iteration/playtest process, not just generate more output.

comments.author: Useful_Use_6170
comments.body: I was doing the good ol promp > make game which only made bad games with bugs so someone told me to create a PRD and start with the core gameplay and expand out !!

replies.author: Neon_Senpai
replies.body:
Yeah, that’s exactly the problem I’ve run into too. “Prompt → make game” sounds fun in theory, but without a clear core loop it usually just turns into a buggy toy instead of an actual playable game.

Starting from a PRD or at least a clear gameplay brief makes way more sense — like what the player does every 10 seconds, what the win/lose condition is, what can change between runs, etc. I’m starting to think the AI part is only useful if it helps turn a solid game idea into something testable faster, not if it replaces the design thinking completely.

replies.body: Yeah I didn’t know that made the mistake of using base44 prompt system and spent probably like $100 in credits I could of used towards Ai agents

replies.author: Neon_Senpai
replies.body:
I feel that. It’s frustrating because these tools make it feel like you can just keep prompting your way into a better game, but after a point you’re mostly spending credits to fix problems that came from not having a clear structure at the start.

That’s why I’m starting to think the important part is not just “better prompts,” but having the AI work from a solid brief/PRD, clear core gameplay rules, and maybe smaller controlled tasks instead of trying to build or rewrite the whole thing at once.

AI agents might help more if they’re used around a clear plan, but without that, they can probably burn credits just as fast too. The workflow matters a lot.

replies.author: Neon_Senpai

Yeah, that sounds like the right direction. Slow is probably better than spending credits trying to generate the whole thing at once.

For an RPG/MMO/roguelike idea, I think the core loop matters way more than scope at the start. Even one tiny playable slice can tell you a lot if the player action → reward → progression loop feels fun.

I’d probably test one small repeatable loop first, then expand from there. That feels much safer than building a huge messy project and trying to fix it later.
